Connect to your instance and log in as the local administrator.\\n2. Open the **Driver** tab.\\n4. Choose **Update Driver**. This opens the\\n **Update Driver Software \u2013 Amazon Elastic\\n Network Adapter** dialog box.\\n\\n 1. On the **How do you want to search for driver software?**\\n page, choose **Browse my computer for driver software**.\\n 2. On the **Browse for driver software on your computer** page,\\n choose **Let me pick from a list of device drivers on my computer**,\\n located below the search bar.\\n 3. On the **Select the device driver you want to install for this hardware**\\n page, choose **Have Disk...**.\\n 4. In the **Install from Disk** window, choose\\n **Browse...**, next to the file location from the dropdown list.\\n 5. Most instances in the [Nitro-based](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/WindowsGuide/instance-types.html#ec2-nitro-instances) instance family use the ENA driver for networking and the AWS NVMe driver for storage. Most instances in the Xen-based instance family (non-Nitro) use the AWS PV driver for both network and storage. Some instances use a combination of drivers for storage and networking. For more information on instances and which drivers they use for networking and storage, see [Hypervisor type](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/instance-types.html#instance-hypervisor-type). In the **Summary of networking and storage features** table, **elastic block storage** (**EBS) Only** indicates that the volume uses AWS PV drivers. **NVME EBS** indicates that the instance uses NVMe drivers.\\n\\n**Note:** AWS PV drivers are supported on Windows Server 2008 R2 and later. Windows Server 2003 uses Citrix PV drivers. Windows Server 2008 R2 supports AWS PV version 8.3.4 and earlier and AWS ENA 2.2.3 and earlier. For more information, see [Paravirtual drivers for Windows instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/WindowsGuide/xen-drivers-overview.html).\\n\\nWhen you're upgrading drivers on Windows instances or changing the instance type, see [Migrate to latest generation instance types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/WindowsGuide/migrating-latest-types.html) (Nitro/Xen).\\n\\n**Note:** You can run the following PowerShell command to list the AWS drivers and driver versions running on the Windows instance:\\n\\n```plaintext\\nGet-CimInstance Win32_P\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/ec2-windows-unreachable-after-driver-upgrade\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Checking AWS docs for ENA driver recovery guidance on Windows EC2 instances"}

{"id": "5eae132b-bc00-4465-857b-670ac26aeca1", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "That confirms the diagnosis: a Windows Update driver rollup overwrote the AWS ENA driver with an incompatible/generic one, which is why the "clean" instances (no driver updates applied) are unaffected.

## Immediate fix

**You can't RDP in since networking is down**, so recovery has to happen out-of-band:

1. **Get console access without network:**
   - Easiest: detach the instance's root EBS volume, attach it as a secondary volume to a healthy "rescue" instance, fix the driver offline, then reattach/reboot. Or use **EC2 Serial Console** (if enabled for the VPC/instance) to get a local Administrator shell without network dependency.
2. **Remove the bad driver and restore the correct ENA driver** using `pnputil`, since Windows may have ranked the generic/rollup driver higher in the Driver Store:
   ```powershell
   # List installed driver packages, find the ENA one(s)
   pnputil /enum-drivers

   # Delete the bad/incompatible ENA driver package (use the oemXX.inf name from above)
   pnputil /delete-driver oemXX.inf /uninstall /force
   ```
3. **Reinstall the AWS-signed ENA driver** — either from the AWS PV driver package (if attached as a rescue volume, run the installer against the offline OS) or via Device Manager → Amazon Elastic Network Adapter → Update Driver → Browse → point at the official `ena.inf` from the AWS driver download.
4. Reboot (`Restart-Computer`), reattach as root volume if you used the rescue-volume method, and verify the adapter comes up clean.
5. Confirm the version is **v2.2.3 or later** (recommended minimum) using Device Manager → ENA adapter → Driver tab, or `Get-NetAdapter` / driver properties.

## Preventing recurrence

- **Exclude/hide the ENA driver from Windows Update** so driver rollups stop overwriting it. On Server 2019 this is typically done via Group Policy (`Do not include drivers with Windows Updates`) or WSUS/SCCM driver-update exclusion, rather than per-machine — since you're managing a fleet, a GPO applied to the OU covering these EC2 instances is the durable fix.
- **Pin/manage ENA driver installs centrally**: push the AWS-tested ENA driver version via your golden AMI or configuration management (SSM State Manager / Distributor package) instead of letting Windows Update supply it.
- **Validate AMIs**: bake the current recommended ENA driver into your base AMI so instances launch with a known-good version, and re-validate after any Windows Update driver rollup is approved in your patch rings.
- **Test patch rings before fleet-wide rollout**: since the "skipped" instances are fine, this points to your patch cycle not excluding driver updates for a canary/test ring first — catching this on a single canary instance before broad rollout would have caught it.

Want me to look into whether EC2 Serial Console is already enabled for this instance/VPC, or check the instance's current ENA driver version via Systems Manager if it has an SSM agent reachable through another path?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
